levels.name: Grade 7–9
levels.summary: Grade 7 to 9 is where gaps start, and where they are cheapest to fix. We rebuild number sense, algebra and basic science carefully, with short homework checked every week, so students sit the NCE with confidence and start Grade 10 with nothing to catch up on.

levels.name: Grade 10–11
levels.summary: Two years, one set of papers. We finish the Cambridge O Level syllabus by Term 2 of Grade 11 and spend the rest of the time on timed past papers, mark schemes and examiner reports, so students know what each paper rewards and where their marks usually leak.

levels.name: Grade 12–13
levels.summary: A Level papers reward method that is quick and clean. Lessons move briskly, every week ends with exam-style questions marked to the Cambridge scheme, and groups stay at twelve or fewer. University and scholarship deadlines are planned from the first term of Grade 12.

method.title: Live lesson
method.text: Ninety minutes on weekdays, two hours on Saturdays; in the room, on Zoom, or both at once. One topic, taught from first principles, then worked examples at exam pace. Questions are expected and cameras stay on.

method.title: Replay the same evening
method.text: The recording and the board notes go into the class folder before 21:30. Students who missed the lesson, or only half followed it, watch it before they start the homework.

method.title: Homework, marked
method.text: A short set after every lesson, handed in on paper or as photos. It comes back within 48 hours with marks in the margin and one line on what to fix first.

method.title: Past-paper drill
method.text: Once a week, a timed section of a real Cambridge paper, marked against the official mark scheme. Grade 7–9 groups do NCE-style questions instead. This is where exam technique is learnt, while mistakes are still cheap.

method.title: A note home
method.text: At the end of each month, parents get a short WhatsApp note: attendance, homework marks, the latest paper score and the one thing to work on next. No jargon, and no surprises at report time.

courses.title: Mathematics
courses.summary: Number, algebra and geometry built carefully, so Grade 10 is not spent catching up.
courses.description:
Most trouble at SC starts here: fractions that were never quite understood, negative numbers handled by guesswork, algebra learnt as a set of tricks. This group goes back over each idea slowly enough that it sticks, then practises it until it is automatic.

Two lessons a week in Room B, about twenty minutes of homework a night, and a ten-question test every Friday. Parents see the marks each month, with a line on what changed. By the end of Grade 9 students should be ready for the NCE and, more usefully, for O Level Mathematics.

courses.title: Science
courses.summary: Biology, chemistry and physics taught together, with a simple practical most Saturdays.
courses.description:
Lower-secondary science covers a lot of ground thinly. We slow it down: one topic per Saturday, a small practical to anchor it, and the key vocabulary written out until students use it correctly without being reminded.

The two-hour session leaves time to redo the week's school homework if it went badly. Grade 9 students move on to NCE-style questions from Term 2, so the format is familiar long before the exam.

courses.title: Mathematics
courses.summary: The full O Level syllabus by Term 2 of Grade 11, then past papers until the exam.
courses.description:
Two lessons a week, one topic at a time, in the order that makes the next topic easier: algebra before graphs, similar triangles before trigonometry. Each lesson ends with exam questions on that topic, marked before the next one.

From Term 2 of Grade 11 the group switches to full papers under time: Paper 1 without a calculator, Paper 2 with one. Every student keeps an error log, and the last month is spent on whatever it shows. Most lost marks come from a handful of repeated mistakes; the point is to find yours early.

courses.title: Additional Mathematics
courses.summary: For students who find 4024 comfortable and want calculus before Grade 12.
courses.description:
Add Maths moves fast and assumes the algebra is solid. We check that in the first fortnight and fill any gaps before starting functions and logarithms. After that, each two-hour Saturday lesson covers one topic in full: the theory, worked examples, and a set of past-paper questions done in the room.

It is worth taking alongside 4024 if A Level Mathematics or Physics is on the cards. The overlap with Pure Mathematics 1 is large, and students who have done 4037 usually start Grade 12 a term ahead.

courses.title: Physics
courses.summary: The idea first, then the formula, then the exam question it turns up in.
courses.description:
O Level Physics rewards students who can explain as well as calculate. Every topic starts with a demonstration or a sketch, moves to the equation, and finishes with the kind of question that asks why. Units and significant figures are checked on every piece of homework, because that is where easy marks go.

Practical skills are taught through the alternative-to-practical paper: reading scales, drawing tables, spotting sources of error. Two lessons a week, in Room A or on Zoom.

courses.title: Chemistry
courses.summary: Moles, bonding and organic chemistry, with the calculations practised until they are routine.
courses.description:
Students who struggle with chemistry are usually struggling with three things: the mole, balancing equations, and remembering which test gives which result. We teach those three early and come back to them every few weeks, so they are fluent by Grade 11.

Lessons are in person because chemistry needs a bench now and then. Simple practicals such as titrations, rates and tests for ions are done in pairs, and each one is written up the way Cambridge expects on the practical papers.

courses.title: Biology
courses.summary: A large syllabus made manageable: one system at a time, and the wording mark schemes want.
courses.description:
Biology is the subject where students know a lot and still lose marks, usually through loose wording. Each topic is paired with the exact phrases mark schemes reward, such as "partially permeable" and "down a concentration gradient", and homework is marked for language as much as content.

One two-hour Saturday session, in Room B or on Zoom. Each term ends with a full past paper and a one-to-one look at the result.
topics: Cells and movement into and out of cells

courses.title: Accounting
courses.summary: Double entry until it is second nature, then the final accounts that carry the marks.
courses.description:
This is Cambridge O Level Accounting, still called Principles of Accounts in most schools. It is a subject of habits. Students who learn double entry properly in Grade 10 find the rest straightforward; students who memorise layouts struggle as soon as a question is worded differently. So the first term goes on the ledger, the books of prime entry and the trial balance, and we do not hurry it.

Grade 11 covers financial statements, year-end adjustments, partnerships and ratio analysis, with a past-paper question in every lesson. Lessons are on Zoom, and worked answers are shared as PDFs the same evening.
topics: Trial balance and correction of errors
Depreciation and disposal of non-current assets
Financial statements of sole traders and partnerships

courses.title: Computer Science
courses.summary: Theory, pseudocode and Python, aimed squarely at the two papers Cambridge sets.
courses.description:
Paper 1 is computer systems: data representation, networks, hardware, security. Paper 2 is algorithms, programming and logic, and it is where most marks are won or lost. At least half of every lesson is spent writing and tracing code, first in Cambridge pseudocode and then in Python.

One 90-minute lesson a week, online, so screens can be shared and code run live. Students need a laptop for this course; a tablet is not enough. Homework includes a short program every week, checked line by line.

courses.title: English Language
courses.summary: Reading closely, summarising tightly and writing to a plan.
courses.description:
1123 has two papers, Reading and Writing, and both are won on method more than flair. Students learn to find the answer in the passage and put it in their own words, to summarise within the word limit, and to plan a composition in a few minutes before writing it.

One lesson a week online, plus one piece of writing marked each week with corrections in the margin. Students then rewrite their weakest paragraph, which is often where they improve most.

courses.title: Mathematics
courses.summary: Pure 1 and 3, Mechanics and Statistics 1, over two years at A Level pace.
courses.description:
Grade 12 covers Pure Mathematics 1 and Probability & Statistics 1; Grade 13 covers Pure Mathematics 3 and Mechanics. Every lesson moves from the idea to a clean worked example to exam questions, and the questions get harder each week rather than each term.

Kavish teaches this group himself and keeps it at twelve. Students chasing a scholarship can take an extra past paper each fortnight, marked to the Cambridge scheme with notes on presentation: at A Level, a correct answer with an unclear method can still lose marks.
topics: Kinematics and Newton's laws of motion

courses.title: Physics
courses.summary: Mechanics, waves and circuits in Grade 12; fields, oscillations and quantum physics in Grade 13.
courses.description:
A Level Physics asks for more mathematics than most students expect: rearranging, logarithms, reading gradients off awkward graphs. We teach that alongside the physics instead of assuming it, which is one reason this group pairs well with 9709.

Paper 3 and Paper 5 are the practical papers, and they are mostly learnable: uncertainties, tables, graph work, planning an experiment. They get a full lesson every month from the start of Grade 12.

courses.title: Chemistry
courses.summary: Physical, inorganic and organic chemistry, with mechanisms drawn until they make sense.
courses.description:
9701 is a big syllabus. We split it into the three strands Cambridge uses, physical, inorganic and organic, and rotate between them so nothing goes cold before the exam. Physical chemistry gets the most calculation practice; organic gets a reaction map that students build themselves over the two years.

Lessons are in Room B with eight students at most, which makes it possible to look at everyone's working, not only the loudest student's. Practical skills for Papers 3 and 5 are covered through data-handling exercises and a few bench experiments each term.

courses.title: Economics
courses.summary: Micro, macro and the essay questions that decide the grade.
courses.description:
A Level Economics comes down to two skills: drawing the right diagram quickly, and writing an argument about it that reaches a judgement. We teach the theory with Mauritian examples, from sugar and textile exports to tourism and the rupee, then practise turning it into twenty-mark essays with a clear conclusion.

Data-response questions get a lesson of their own every month. Essays are marked against the Cambridge levels of response, with a short note on what would have moved the answer up a level.
topics: Exchange rates and the balance of payments

courses.title: Computer Science
courses.summary: AS and A Level Computer Science in Python, with the theory papers taken seriously.
courses.description:
9618 has four papers: two of theory, two of problem-solving and programming. Students who code well tend to underrate the theory, and students who revise theory well often freeze in front of a blank program. Lessons alternate between the two, and every week includes a timed programming task.

We use Python, one of the three languages Cambridge accepts, and Cambridge pseudocode for written answers. Grade 13 covers recursion, object-oriented programming and abstract data types such as stacks, queues and linked lists. Lessons are on Google Meet so code can be shared and run live.

courses.title: General Paper
courses.summary: Essays with a clear argument, and comprehension read carefully.
courses.description:
General Paper is part of the HSC, and it is often the subject students prepare least. The essay paper rewards a clear position, well-chosen examples and control of language; the comprehension paper rewards reading what is actually written. Both can be taught.

One lesson a week online. Every fortnight students write a full essay under time and get it back with margin comments and a mark. The group keeps a shared file of Mauritian and international examples on climate, technology, education and the economy, and adds to it all year.
topics: Current affairs: Mauritius and the world

tutors.name: Kavish
tutors.bio: Kavish has taught Mathematics and Physics since 2012: six years in state secondary schools, then in his own rooms in Quatre Bornes. He still teaches every SC and A Level Mathematics group himself. His lessons are quiet and quick, and built around one question: can you explain why that step works? He added Computer Science in 2019, on the grounds that most of it is mathematics with stricter error messages.
credentials: Six years teaching in state secondary schools

tutors.name: Priya N.
tutors.bio: Priya taught Chemistry and Biology at a secondary school in the centre of the island for four years before joining in 2021. She is strict about language ("the enzyme is denatured", never "the enzyme dies") because that is where science marks quietly disappear. She also runs both Grade 7–9 groups, where she is patient, firm, and known for a ten-question Friday test that nobody minds as much as they claim.

tutors.name: Yannick L.
tutors.bio: Yannick read Economics at the University of Mauritius and spent more time on the debating team than he admits to his students, which is how he came to teach General Paper and SC English alongside Accounting and Economics. He joined in 2022 after three years at a private secondary school, and teaches mostly online. His feedback is short: what worked, what to cut, and what to try next time.

quiz.title: Where should you start?
quiz.intro: Questions in maths, science, commerce and computing, from Grade 7 to A Level, getting harder as you go. There is no timer and no sign-up. If you haven't met a topic yet, make a sensible guess and move on.

questions.explain: Divide by 4 to find one quarter, which is 14, then multiply by 3: 42.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.explain: Rusting makes a new substance, iron oxide. The other three are physical changes: nothing new is made, and each can be reversed.

questions.prompt: A school bag costs Rs 2,400. In a sale it is 15% off. What is the sale price?
questions.explain: 15% of 2,400 is 360. Take that off the price: 2,400 − 360 = Rs 2,040.

questions.prompt: What is the binary number 1011 in denary?
questions.explain: The place values are 8, 4, 2 and 1, so 1011 means 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

questions.prompt: In a plant cell, where does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs the light energy photosynthesis needs.
The highest common factor of both terms is 3x, which leaves 3x(2x − 5). Taking out only 3, or only x, is correct but not fully factorised.

questions.prompt: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s².

questions.prompt: Which of these is a credit balance in a trial balance?
questions.explain: Capital is what the business owes its owner, so it is a credit balance. Drawings, purchases and assets such as machinery are debit balances.

questions.prompt: What is the gradient of the line through (1, 2) and (4, 11)?
questions.explain: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x = (11 − 2) ÷ (4 − 1) = 9 ÷ 3 = 3.

questions.prompt: How many moles are there in 22 g of carbon dioxide? (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is CO2, so its Mr is 12 + 2 × 16 = 44. Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 22 ÷ 44 = 0.5 mol.

questions.prompt: How many bits are needed to give each of 200 colours its own binary code?
questions.explain: 7 bits give only 128 different codes, which is not enough. 8 bits give 256, which covers 200.

questions.prompt: A trader buys goods for Rs 800 and sells them for Rs 1,000. What is the profit margin?
questions.explain: Margin compares profit with the selling price: 200 ÷ 1,000 = 20%. 25% is the mark-up, which compares profit with cost.

questions.prompt: Differentiate y = x³ − 4x² + 7 with respect to x.
questions.explain: Multiply each term by its power and reduce the power by one: 3x² − 8x. The constant 7 differentiates to zero.

questions.prompt: A wire is replaced by one of the same metal, twice as long and with half the cross-sectional area. What happens to the resistance?
options: It becomes four times as large
questions.explain: Resistance = resistivity × length ÷ area. Doubling the length doubles it, and halving the area doubles it again: 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.prompt: The price of a good rises by 10% and the quantity demanded falls by 5%. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explain: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price = −5 ÷ 10 = −0.5. Its size is less than 1, so demand is price-inelastic.

questions.prompt: Find the integral of 2x + 1 from x = 0 to x = 2.
questions.explain: Integrate to get x² + x. At x = 2 that is 6, and at x = 0 it is 0, so the answer is 6 − 0 = 6.

questions.prompt: What is the pH of hydrochloric acid with a concentration of 0.010 mol/dm³?
questions.explain: HCl is a strong acid and fully dissociates, so [H+] = 0.010 mol/dm³. pH = −log(0.010) = 2.

questions.prompt: What is the denary value of the 8-bit two's complement number 11111010?
questions.explain: In two's complement the leftmost bit is worth −128, so the value is −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 = −6.

results.title: Start with the foundations
results.text: Several of the basics are not automatic yet, and that is what costs marks later. A term in a Grade 7–9 group, or a slower start at SC, will fix it faster than pushing on. Book a free trial lesson and we will confirm the right group.

results.title: Ready for SC work
results.text: The core skills are mostly there. What is missing is accuracy under time and knowing what each question wants, and that is what an SC group with a weekly past-paper drill is for. Already in Grade 12? Expect to revisit a few O Level topics early on.

results.title: Working at A Level pace
results.text: You handled the harder questions with clean method. An HSC group will suit you: the work there is depth and speed. Choose your subjects and come to a free trial lesson.

faqs.q: Can my child try a lesson before we pay?
faqs.a: Yes. The first lesson in any group is free, in the room or on Zoom. Hand in the homework from that lesson too: seeing how it comes back marked is the quickest way to judge us. If the group turns out to be the wrong level, we will say so and suggest another.

faqs.q: What happens if my child misses a lesson?
faqs.a: Every lesson is recorded. The recording and the board notes go into the class folder the same evening, and homework is still marked if it comes in a day or two late. If a cyclone or torrential rain warning closes schools, the lesson goes ahead on Zoom at the usual time.
Twelve students at most for SC and HSC, fourteen for Grade 7–9, and several groups are smaller. Students joining on Zoom count towards the same limit, so a hybrid group never quietly doubles in size.

Yes. Pay monthly or per term by MCB Juice or bank transfer; the details are on the Plans page. Please use the student's full name as the reference. Fees are due in the first week of the month, and a receipt comes back on WhatsApp.

faqs.q: How will I know whether it is working?
faqs.a: At the end of each month you get a short WhatsApp note: attendance, homework marks, the latest past-paper score and one thing to work on next. Twice a year we also meet you, or call, for fifteen minutes to go through the papers together.

faqs.q: Which syllabus versions do you teach?
faqs.a: The Cambridge syllabus your child will actually sit: 4024 for SC Mathematics, 9709 for A Level, and so on. When Cambridge revises a syllabus we teach the new version and mark which topics were added or dropped, so older past papers are used sensibly. Grade 7–9 groups follow the national curriculum and prepare for the NCE.

faqs.q: What does my child need for online lessons?
faqs.a: A laptop or tablet with a camera, a steady internet connection and a quiet corner. A phone screen is too small for past papers. Homework can be handed in as photos, so there is no need for a scanner. Computer Science students need a laptop.

faqs.q: What if we need to stop?
faqs.a: Tell us before the last week of the month and you will not be charged for the next one. Termly payments are refunded for any full months not yet started, less the termly discount. There is no deposit and no contract.
